Regular sequences of power sums and complete symmetric polynomialsThanks: Date: October 0707, 20112011.Thanks: Key words: Regular sequences, Symmetric polynomials. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: Primary 05​E​0505E05; Secondary 13​P​10, 11​C​0813P10,\;11C08.

Neeraj Kumar Address: Dipartimento di Matematica, Universitá di Genova
Via Dodecaneso 35, 16146 Genova, Italy Email address: kumar@dima.unige.it and Ivan Martino Address: Matematiska Institutionen, Stockholms Universitet, Stockholm, Sweden Email address: martino@math.su.se
Abstract.

In this article, we carry out the investigation for regular sequences of symmetric polynomials in the polynomial ring in three and four variable. Any two power sum element in ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}] for n≥3n\geq 3 always form a regular sequence and we state the conjecture when pa,pb,pcp_{a},p_{b},p_{c} for given positive integers a<b<ca<b<c forms a regular sequence in ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3,x4]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}]. We also provide evidence for this conjecture by proving it in special instances. We also prove that any sequence of power sums of the form pa,pa+1,…,pa+m−1,pbp_{a},p_{a+1},\dots,p_{a+m-1},p_{b} with m<n−1m<n-1 forms a regular sequence in ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}]. We also provide a partial evidence in support of conjecture’s given by Conca, Krattenthaler and Watanabe in [1] on regular sequences of symmetric polynomials.

1. Introduction

The work in this article is inspired by the work of Conca, Krattenthaler and Watanabe on regular sequences of symmetric polynomials [1].

We introduce some basic definitions, notation and well known results which we will use in the sequel. Let S=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]S=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] be a polynomial ring. We denote by pm​(x1,x2,…,xn),hm​(x1,x2,…,xn)p_{m}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}),h_{m}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}) and em​(x1,x2,…,xn)e_{m}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}), the power sum symmetric polynomials, complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials and the elementary symmetric polynomials of degree mm in SS respectively, that is:

pm​(x1,x2,…,xn):=∑i=1nxim,hm​(x1,x2,…,xn):=∑1≤i1≤i2≤⋯≤im≤nxi1xi2⋯xim,em​(x1,x2,…,xn):=∑1≤i1<i2<⋯<im≤nxi1xi2⋯xim.\begin{split}p_{m}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}):=&\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{m},\\ h_{m}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}):=&\sum_{1\leq i_{1}\leq i_{2}\leq\cdots\leq i_{m}\leq n}x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\cdots x_{i_{m}},\\ e_{m}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}):=&\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{m}\leq n}x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\cdots x_{i_{m}}.\end{split}

We will also denote by pm​(n),hm​(n), and ​em​(n),p_{m}(n),\;h_{m}(n),\text{ and }e_{m}(n), the power sum symmetric polynomials, complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials, and the elementary symmetric polynomials respectively. When nn is clear from the context, we may simply denote them by pm,hm​ and ​emp_{m},h_{m}\text{ and }e_{m} respectively.

A sequence of elements f1,f2,…,fkf_{1},f_{2},\dots,f_{k} in SS is a regular sequence on SS if the ideal (f1,f2,…,fk)(f_{1},f_{2},\dots,f_{k}) is proper and for each ii, the image of fi+1f_{i+1} is a nonzero divisor in S/(f1,…,fi)S/(f_{1},\dots,f_{i}).

We have used Newton’s formulas for pn,hn​ and ​enp_{n},h_{n}\text{ and }e_{n}, ( see equation 2.6′,2.11′2.6^{\prime},2.11^{\prime}) from Macdonald [3]. These relations together with the Theorem 2.2 are very helpful in investigating regular sequences.

We have used the Serre’s criterion for normality (see section 18.318.3, Theorem 18.1518.15 [2]) for proving primeness for power sum polynomials in the polynomial ring. Once we know that pa,pbp_{a},p_{b} generates a prime ideal in ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3,x4]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}], we can add one more polynomial ff and conclude that pa,pb,fp_{a},p_{b},f forms a regular sequence for all f∉(pa,pb)f\notin(p_{a},p_{b}). We prove p1,p2​mp_{1},p_{2m} generates a prime ideal, where m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, see Proposition 4.7. We also prove this in the case of consecutive integres a,a+1a,a+1. In fact we prove a more general statement that any consecutive power sum pa,pa+1,…,pa+m−1p_{a},p_{a+1},\dots,p_{a+m-1} with m<n−1m<n-1 generates a prime ideal in ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}], see Theorem 4.4.

In general, it turns out to be difficult to find conditions on {a,b}\{a,b\} such that (pa,pb)(p_{a},p_{b}) is a prime ideal. We did several computations in CoCoA and found some conditions on {a,b}\{a,b\} such that (pa,pb)(p_{a},p_{b}) is a prime ideal, see Conjecture 4.9. For example when aa is prime number, a≥5a\geq 5 and b=a+m+6​db=a+m+6d with m∈{1,5}m\in\{1,5\} then (pa,pb)(p_{a},p_{b}) is a prime ideal.

However, a very nice introduction to regular sequences of symmetric polynomials is given by Conca, Krattenthaler and Watanabe in [1]. So, we refer the reader for detailed introduction to [1].

Convention: By an expression of the form fi1,fi2,…,fikf_{i_{1}},f_{i_{2}},\dots,f_{i_{k}} or (fi1,fi2,…​fik)(f_{i_{1}},f_{i_{2}},\dots f_{i_{k}}) for the power sum and complete symmetric polynomials, we always assume that i1<i2<⋯<iki_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{k}.

2. Some results on regular sequences

Let us recall some well known results about regular sequences.

Lemma 2.1.

Let S=ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]S=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}] be a polynomial ring. The sequence of homogeneous polynomials f1,f2,…,fkf_{1},f_{2},\dots,f_{k} is a regular sequence in SS if and only if

HS/I​(z)=∏i=1k(1−zdi)(1−z)n.H_{S/I}(z)=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{k}(1-z^{d_{i}})}{(1-z)^{n}}.

where di=deg⁡fid_{i}=\deg{f_{i}} and I=(f1,f2,…,fk).I=(f_{1},f_{2},\dots,f_{k}).

We will use the following characterization very often for proving regular sequence for the power sums and complete symmetric polynomials:

Theorem 2.2.

Let fi,fj,fk∈S=ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3]f_{i},f_{j},f_{k}\in S=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}]. The sequence fi,fj,fkf_{i},f_{j},f_{k} is a regular sequence if and only if fk∉(fi,fj)f_{k}\notin(f_{i},f_{j}) and for any ff of degree bigger than i+j+ki+j+k we have f∈(fi,fj,fk)f\in(f_{i},f_{j},f_{k}).

Proof.

If fi,fj,fkf_{i},f_{j},f_{k} is a regular sequence then fif_{i} is not a zero divisor on SS, fjf_{j} is not a zero divisor on S/(fi)S/(f_{i}) and fkf_{k} is not a zero divisor on S/(fi,fj)S/(f_{i},f_{j}). This implies fk∉(fi,fj)f_{k}\notin(f_{i},f_{j}).

We know that (0,0,0)(0,0,0) is the only solution of the system (fi,fj,fk)(f_{i},f_{j},f_{k}). This means (0,0,0)(0,0,0) has multiplicity i+j+ki+j+k and (fi,fj,fk)(f_{i},f_{j},f_{k}) is the (i+j+k)(i+j+k)-th power of the maximal ideal. So considering ff with degree of ff bigger than i+j+ki+j+k, this implies f∈(fi,fj,fk)f\in(f_{i},f_{j},f_{k}). ∎

Of course, there are three possible cases for fi,fj,fkf_{i},f_{j},f_{k} in ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}]:

  1. (a)

    fk∉(fi,fj)f_{k}\notin(f_{i},f_{j}), and fi,fj,fkf_{i},f_{j},f_{k} is a regular sequence;

  2. (b)

    fk∉(fi,fj)f_{k}\notin(f_{i},f_{j}), and fi,fj,fkf_{i},f_{j},f_{k} is not a regular sequence,

  3. (c)

    fk∈(fi,fj)f_{k}\in(f_{i},f_{j}), then fi,fj,fkf_{i},f_{j},f_{k} is not a regular sequence.

See an Example 5.1, where hk∉(hi,hj)h_{k}\notin(h_{i},h_{j}) and hi,hj,hkh_{i},h_{j},h_{k} is not a regular sequence.

For a subset A⊂ℕ∗A\subset\mathbb{N}^{*}, we set

pA​(n)={pa​(n):a∈A}​ and ​hA​(n)={ha​(n):a∈A}.p_{A}(n)=\{p_{a}(n):a\in A\}\text{ and }h_{A}(n)=\{h_{a}(n):a\in A\}.

Let A⊂ℕ∗A\subset\mathbb{N}^{*} be a set of nn consecutive elements. Then both pA​(n)p_{A}(n) and hA​(n)h_{A}(n) are regular sequences in k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

Let pnp_{n} be the power sum symmetric polynomial of degree nn, hnh_{n} be the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial of degree nn and let ene_{n} be the elementary symmetric polynomial of degree nn. Then

n​en=∑i=1n(−1)i−1​en−i​pi​ for all n≥1. and ∑i=0n(−1)i​ei​hn−i=0​ for all n≥1. \begin{split}ne_{n}=&\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{i-1}e_{n-i}p_{i}\text{ for all $n\geq 1.$ }\\ \text{and }&\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^{i}e_{i}h_{n-i}=0\text{ for all $n\geq 1.$ }\end{split}

These equations are due to Isaac Newton, see Macdonald [3] ( equation 2.6′,2.11′2.6^{\prime},2.11^{\prime}).

3. Symmetric Polynomials in 33 variables

3.1. Power Sums in 33 variables

Conjecture 3.1.

(Conca, Krattenthaler, Watanabe)
Let a,b,ca,b,c be positive integers with a<b<ca<b<c and gcd⁡(a,b,c)=1\gcd(a,b,c)=1. Then pa,pb,pcp_{a},p_{b},p_{c} is a regular sequence if and only if a​b​c≡0(mod6)abc\equiv 0(\mod 6).

Remark 3.2.

For this conjecture, the “only if” part has been proved in [1], they provide partial result in support of the “if” part. We have also tried to prove this in some special cases, here the only difference is in approach, we provide a nice expression for pcmod(pa,pb)p_{c}\mod(p_{a},p_{b}).

Consider the power sum sequence p1,p2,pnp_{1},p_{2},p_{n}, then

pn={3​e3kmod(p1,p2), if n=3​k;0mod(p1,p2), otherwise.p_{n}=\begin{cases}3e_{3}^{k}\mod(p_{1},p_{2}),&\text{ if $n=3k$;}\\ 0\mod(p_{1},p_{2}),&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}
Proof.

As p0=3p_{0}=3, we use Newtons formula, see Proposition 2.4 to write pnp_{n}.

p1=e1=0,p2=e1​p1−2​e2=0⟹e2=0,p3=3​e3+e1​p2−e2​p1=3​e3,p4=e1p3−e2p2+e3p1=0, similarly p5=0,p6=3​e32. And so on, we continue this way.\begin{split}p_{1}=&e_{1}=0,\\ p_{2}=&e_{1}p_{1}-2e_{2}=0\implies e_{2}=0,\\ p_{3}=&3e_{3}+e_{1}p_{2}-e_{2}p_{1}=3e_{3},\\ p_{4}=&e_{1}p_{3}-e_{2}p_{2}+e_{3}p_{1}=0,\text{ similarly }p_{5}=0,\\ p_{6}=&3e_{3}^{2}.\text{ And so on, we continue this way.}\end{split}

Hence we get pn=3​e3kmod(p1,p2)p_{n}=3e_{3}^{k}\mod(p_{1},p_{2}) if n=3​kn=3k.

∎

Corollary 3.4.

p1,p2,pnp_{1},p_{2},p_{n} is a regular sequence if and only if n=3​k,k∈ℕ.n=3k,k\in\mathbb{N}.

Proof.

We only need to verify the cases of the form p1,p2,pnp_{1},p_{2},p_{n} where n=3​k,k∈ℕn=3k,k\in\mathbb{N}. Choose any m>1+2+3​k=3​(k+1)m>1+2+3k=3(k+1), we observe that pm∈(p1,p2,pn)p_{m}\in(p_{1},p_{2},p_{n}). Hence p1,p2,pnp_{1},p_{2},p_{n} is a regular sequence for n=3​k,k∈ℕ.n=3k,k\in\mathbb{N}. ∎

Proposition 3.5.

Consider the sequence p1,p3,pnp_{1},p_{3},p_{n}, then

pn={(−1)k​e2kmod(p1,p3), if n=2​k;0mod(p1,p3), otherwise.p_{n}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{k}e_{2}^{k}\mod(p_{1},p_{3}),&\text{ if $n=2k$;}\\ 0\mod(p_{1},p_{3}),&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}
Proof.

Similar to Proposition 3.3. ∎

Corollary 3.6.

p1,p3,pnp_{1},p_{3},p_{n} is a regular sequence if and only if n=2​k,k∈ℕ.n=2k,k\in\mathbb{N}.

Proof.

Similar to Corollary 3.4. ∎

Remark 3.7.

p2,p3,pnp_{2},p_{3},p_{n} is a regular sequence for all nn, see Theorem 2.112.11 [1]. In the paper [1], they have given a complete proof. We present here the slightly tricky argument from their paper, they managed to reduce the problem and concluded that it is enough to prove this for the case n=4n=4. They did computer experiments to show this for n=4n=4 case. But it follows directly from Proposition 2.92.9 [1] as 2,3,42,3,4 are consecutive integers.

Let A={a,b,c}A=\{a,b,c\} with a<b<ca<b<c. Then ha,hb,hch_{a},h_{b},h_{c} is a regular sequence if and only if the following conditions are satisfied:

4. Symmetric Polynomials in 44 variables

4.1. Power sums in 44 variables

Theorem 4.1.

Let pip_{i} be the power sum symmetric polynomials of degree ii in the polynomial ring S=ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]S=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}]. Let n≥3n\geq 3, then pa,pbp_{a},p_{b} is a regular sequence.

Proof.

We know pa​(n)p_{a}(n) is reducible for n=1n=1 and p2​(n)p_{2}(n) is reducible for n=2n=2. For n≥3n\geq 3, we will show pa​(n)p_{a}(n) is an irreducible element. We prove this by induction on nn. For n=3n=3, we can write pa​(3)=x3a+gp_{a}(3)=x_{3}^{a}+g, where g=x1a+x2a∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2]g=x_{1}^{a}+x_{2}^{a}\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2}], gg is a homogeneous and monic polynomial in both variable, of degree aa. So proving factorization of g⁡(x1,x2)g(x_{1},x_{2}) is same as proving factorization of g⁡(x1,1)g(x_{1},1). Since g⁡(x1,1)g(x_{1},1) has simple roots, gg is a product of a linear forms. Thus Lemma 2.5 shows that pa​(3)p_{a}(3) is irreducible. Then, if n>3n>3, pa​(n)=xna+pa​(n−1)p_{a}(n)=x_{n}^{a}+p_{a}(n-1) is irreducible by Lemma 2.5 by induction. Therefore the ideal generated by pap_{a} is a prime ideal. Hence S/(pa)S/(p_{a}) is a domain. Now pbp_{b} being an irreducible element in SS, can not be factored into lower degree power sum polynomials pap_{a}. So pbp_{b} is a non zero divisor on S/(pa)S/(p_{a}) for b>ab>a. Hence pa,pbp_{a},p_{b} is a regular sequence. ∎

Note 4.2.

If the characteristic of base field 𝕂\mathbb{K} is not zero, then above result does not hold. Consider the field with char⁡(𝕂)=2\operatorname{char}(\mathbb{K})=2, then one has p4=p22p_{4}=p_{2}^{2}.

In particular,

Proposition 4.3.

Let pip_{i} be the power sum symmetric polynomials of degree ii in the polynomial ring S=ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3,x4]S=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}]. Then pa,pbp_{a},p_{b} is a regular sequence.

We know that a subset of a regular sequence is a regular sequence. So by Proposition 2.3, pa,pa+1,…,pa+m−1p_{a},p_{a+1},\dots,p_{a+m-1} is a regular sequence. Let R=S/IR={S}/{I}, where S=ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]S=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}], I=⟨pa,pa+1,…,pa+m−1⟩I=\langle p_{a},p_{a+1},\dots,p_{a+m-1}\rangle with m<n−1m<n-1. Hence RR is Cohen Macaulay. Now we are going to use the Serre Criterion (see section 18.318.3, Theorem 18.1518.15 [2]) for proving mm consecutive power sum polynomials generates a prime ideal in the polynomial ring SS. Once we know that II is a prime ideal in SS, we can add one more power sum element pcp_{c} and conclude that pa,pa+1,…,pa+m−1,pcp_{a},p_{a+1},\dots,p_{a+m-1},p_{c} forms a regular sequence provided pc∉Ip_{c}\notin I.

Theorem 4.4.

Let pip_{i} be the power sum symmetric polynomials of degree ii in the polynomial ring S=ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]S=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}], with n≥4n\geq 4.
Then I=⟨pa,pa+1,…,pa+m−1⟩I=\langle p_{a},p_{a+1},\dots,p_{a+m-1}\rangle with m<n−1m<{n-1} is a prime ideal in SS. In particular, pa,pa+1,…,pa+m−1,pcp_{a},p_{a+1},\dots,p_{a+m-1},p_{c} forms a regular sequence provided pc∉I.p_{c}\notin I.

Proof.

Consider S=ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]S=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}], I=(pa,pa+1,…,pa+m−1)I=(p_{a},p_{a+1},\dots,p_{a+m-1}) with m<n−1m<n-1 and R=S/IR={S}/{I}. Now let us compute the Jacobian of II, say Jacobian:=J:=J.

J=c​(x1a−1x2a−1⋯xna−1x1ax2a⋯xna⋯x1a+m−2x2a+m−2⋯xna+m−2)J=c\begin{pmatrix}x_{1}^{a-1}&x_{2}^{a-1}&\cdots&x_{n}^{a-1}\\ x_{1}^{a}&x_{2}^{a}&\cdots&x_{n}^{a}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\cdots&\vdots\\ x_{1}^{a+m-2}&x_{2}^{a+m-2}&\cdots&x_{n}^{a+m-2}\\ \end{pmatrix}

We have taken the coefficients out from each row, where c=∏i=0m−1(a+i)c=\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}(a+i). We can ignore the coefficients since we are in the field of characteristic zero and cc is a unit in ℂ\mathbb{C}. Let J′=Im​(J)J^{\prime}=I_{m}(J), denote’s the ideal generated by m×mm\times m minors of Jacobian. Also m=ht​(I)m=\text{ht}(I), since II is generated by a regular sequence of length mm. The m×mm\times m submatrices of the jacobian are standard Van der monde matrices, we know their determinants. So we can write

J′=⟨xi1j1xi2j2⋯ximjm∏1≤a<b≤m(xia−xib)⟩ for 1≤i1<i2<⋯<im≤n,J^{\prime}=\langle\;x_{i_{1}}^{j_{1}}x_{i_{2}}^{j_{2}}\cdots x_{i_{m}}^{j_{m}}\prod_{1\leq a<b\leq m}(x_{i_{a}}-x_{i_{b}})\;\rangle\text{ for }1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{m}\leq n,

and for some positive integers j1,j2,…,jmj_{1},j_{2},\dots,j_{m}. Therefore

I+J′=⟨pa,pa+1,…,pa+m−1,xi1j1xi2j2⋯ximjm∏1≤a<b≤m(xia−xib)⟩.I+J^{\prime}=\langle p_{a},p_{a+1},\dots,p_{a+m-1},\;x_{i_{1}}^{j_{1}}x_{i_{2}}^{j_{2}}\cdots x_{i_{m}}^{j_{m}}\prod_{1\leq a<b\leq m}(x_{i_{a}}-x_{i_{b}})\rangle.

Claim: I+J′=(x1,x2,…,xn).\sqrt{I+J^{\prime}}=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}).
Suppose not, that is, there exists w∈ℙn−1w\in\mathbb{P}^{n-1} with w∈Z⁡(I+J′)w\in Z(I+J^{\prime}). Then the vector ww can have at the most m−1m-1 distinct non zero coordinates. If ww has mm or more than mm distinct non zero coordinates, then w∉Z⁡(J′)w\notin Z(J^{\prime}). Say ww has vv distinct non zero coordinates. We can write

w=(w1,…​w1,w2,…,w2,…,wv,…,wv,0,0,…,0),w=(w_{1},\dots w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{2},\dots,w_{v},\dots,w_{v},0,0,\dots,0),

where wiw_{i} appears βi\beta_{i} times and v≤m−1v\leq{m-1}. Also ww should satisfy pa+ip_{a+i} for i=0,1,…,m−1i=0,1,\dots,m-1 i.e.

β1​w1a+i+β2​w2a+i+⋯+βv​wva+i=0​ for i=1,2,…,m. \beta_{1}w_{1}^{a+i}+\beta_{2}w_{2}^{a+i}+\cdots+\beta_{v}w_{v}^{a+i}=0\text{ for $i=1,2,\dots,m.$ }

This is a system of equation, which can be represented in the matrix form with mm rows, vv column.

(11⋯1w1w2⋯wv⋯w1m−1w2m−1⋯wvm−1)​(β1​w1a+iβ2​w2a+iβv​wva+i)=(000)\begin{pmatrix}1&1&\cdots&1\\ w_{1}&w_{2}&\cdots&w_{v}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\cdots&\vdots\\ w_{1}^{m-1}&w_{2}^{m-1}&\cdots&w_{v}^{m-1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\beta_{1}w_{1}^{a+i}\\ \beta_{2}w_{2}^{a+i}\\ \vdots\\ \beta_{v}w_{v}^{a+i}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\\ \vdots\\ 0\end{pmatrix}

We know that neither βi=0\beta_{i}=0 nor wi=0w_{i}=0 for i=1,…,vi=1,\dots,v. So, βi​wia+i≠0\beta_{i}w_{i}^{a+i}\neq 0 for i=1,…,vi=1,\dots,v. We can choose the matrix say MM with first vv rows out of mm rows and look for the solution. The matrix MM is of full rank since wi≠wjw_{i}\neq w_{j} for i≠ji\neq j, so the only possible solution has to be the trivial solution.

Therefore such a ww does not exist and hence the claim is proved. This implies ht​(I+J′)=n\text{ht}(I+J^{\prime})=n and dimSI+J′=0\dim\frac{S}{I+J^{\prime}}=0. The co-dimension of J′J^{\prime} in SS is n−2n-2. Hence by Theorem 18.1518.15 in [2], RR is a product of normal domain. So, we can write R=R1×⋯×RkR=R_{1}\times\cdots\times R_{k}. Since RR is a standard graded ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra with R0=ℂR_{0}=\mathbb{C}, also R0=(R1)0×⋯×(Rk)0=ℂkR_{0}=(R_{1})_{0}\times\cdots\times(R_{k})_{0}=\mathbb{C}^{k}. Hence k=1k=1. Therefore RR is a normal domain and II is a prime ideal in SS. ∎

In particular,

Proposition 4.5.

Let pip_{i} be the power sum symmetric polynomials of degree ii in the polynomial ring S=ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3,x4]S=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}]; then I=(pi,pi+1)I=(p_{i},p_{i+1}) is a prime ideal in SS. In particular, pi,pi+1,pnp_{i},p_{i+1},p_{n} is a regular sequence for all pn∉(pi,pi+1)p_{n}\notin(p_{i},p_{i+1}).

Lemma 4.6.

Let n≥5n\geq 5 be any natural number. If the sum of four distinct nn-th roots of unity is zero, then they must be two pair of opposite sign.

Furthermore, if nn is odd number, then sum of four distinct nn-th roots of unity is never zero.

Proof.

We have zn=1z^{n}=1. Let us pick four distinct nn-th roots of unity, call it zjz_{j} for j=1,2,3,4j=1,2,3,4. Each zj=xj+i​yjz_{j}=x_{j}+iy_{j}, where xj,yj∈ℝx_{j},y_{j}\in\mathbb{R} and |zj|=1|z_{j}|=1.
Claim: If ∑j=14zj=0\sum_{j=1}^{4}z_{j}=0, then z1,z2,z3,z4z_{1},\;z_{2},\;z_{3},\;z_{4} must be of the form z1,z2,−z1,−z2.z_{1},\;z_{2},\;-z_{1},\;-z_{2}.
Let ∑j=14zj=0\sum_{j=1}^{4}z_{j}=0 i.e. ∑j=14xj=0\sum_{j=1}^{4}x_{j}=0 and ∑j=14yj=0\sum_{j=1}^{4}y_{j}=0. So, we can write,

x1+x2=−(x3+x4), and ​y1+y2=−(y3+y4).x_{1}+x_{2}=-(x_{3}+x_{4}),\text{ and }y_{1}+y_{2}=-(y_{3}+y_{4}).

Now, squaring and adding both the equation, we obtain 2+2​(x1​x2+y1​y2)=2+2​(x3​x4+y3​y4)2+2(x_{1}x_{2}+y_{1}y_{2})=2+2(x_{3}x_{4}+y_{3}y_{4}). Therefore, we get,

|z1−z2|2=2−2​(x1​x2+y1​y2)=2−2​(x3​x4+y3​y4)=|z3−z4|2.|z_{1}-z_{2}|^{2}=2-2(x_{1}x_{2}+y_{1}y_{2})=2-2(x_{3}x_{4}+y_{3}y_{4})=|z_{3}-z_{4}|^{2}.

So |z1−z2|=|z3−z4||z_{1}-z_{2}|=|z_{3}-z_{4}|. Similarly, we get |z2−z3|=|z1−z4||z_{2}-z_{3}|=|z_{1}-z_{4}|. So, four distinct zjz_{j} form a parellelogram. The diagonals of a parellelogram intersect at mid point. Hence solving z1+z32=z2+z42\frac{z_{1}+z_{3}}{2}=\frac{z_{2}+z_{4}}{2} and ∑j=14zj=0\sum_{j=1}^{4}z_{j}=0, we conclude that z3=−z1z_{3}=-z_{1} and z4=−z2z_{4}=-z_{2}. So, we obtain four distinct roots of unity as z1,z2,−z1,−z2z_{1},\;z_{2},\;-z_{1},\;-z_{2}.

Furthermore, z1z_{1} and −z1-z_{1} both can not be nn-th roots of unity for any nn odd number. ∎

Proposition 4.7.

Let I=(p1,p2​m)I=(p_{1},p_{2m}), where m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}. Then II is a prime ideal in ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3,x4]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}]. Therefore p1,p2​m,pnp_{1},p_{2m},p_{n} form a regular sequence for all pn∉(p1,p2​m)p_{n}\notin(p_{1},p_{2m}).

Proof.

Suppose not, i.e. there exists w∈ℙ3w\in\mathbb{P}^{3} with w∈Z⁡(I+J)w\in Z(I+J). Let w=(w1,w2,w3,w4)w=(w_{1},w_{2},w_{3},w_{4}). Since ww is in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}, we can make w1=1w_{1}=1 if w1≠0w_{1}\neq 0. So let w=(1,x,y,z)w=(1,x,y,z). 1+x+y+z=0​ and ​1+x2​m+y2​m+z2​m=0.1+x+y+z=0\text{ and }1+x^{2m}+y^{2m}+z^{2m}=0.

5.1. Verification of the Conca, Krattenthaler and Watanabe conjecture

  • (i)

    For p1,p2,pnp_{1},p_{2},p_{n}: This follows directly from Corollary 3.4.

  • (ii)

    For p1,p3,pnp_{1},p_{3},p_{n}: This follows directly from Corollary 3.6.

  • (iii)

    For h1,h2,hnh_{1},h_{2},h_{n}: Let us start with the necessary part.

    1. 1

      2​c≡0(mod6)2c\equiv 0(\mod 6) implies that c=3​kc=3k.

    2. 2

      gcd​(2,3)=1\text{gcd}(2,3)=1 (always true).

    3. 3

      For all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} with t>2t>2 there exist d∈Ad\in A such that d+2≢0,1(modt)d+2\not\equiv 0,1(\mod t): we know that 1+21+2 and 2+22+2 are 00 or 11 only modulo 33 and so t=3; these means that this condition is false iff c+2≅0,1(mod3)c+2\cong 0,1(\mod 3). Thus, we have that c=3​kc=3k.

    Viceversa, if n=3​kn=3k, [1][1] and [3][3] are fulfilled.

Similarly we can show, (i​v)(iv) for h1,h3,hnh_{1},h_{3},h_{n}\;; (v)(v) for h1,h4,hnh_{1},h_{4},h_{n}, and (v​i)(vi) for h2,h3,hnh_{2},h_{3},h_{n} respectively.

Example 5.1.

This example is a case when hk∉(hi,hj)h_{k}\notin(h_{i},h_{j}) and hi,hj,hkh_{i},h_{j},h_{k} is not a regular sequence.

Consider the triple h1,h4,h5,h_{1},h_{4},h_{5}, By Proposition 3.14, we have h5=−e2​e3mod(h1,h4)h_{5}=-e_{2}e_{3}\mod(h_{1},h_{4}), hence h5∉(h1,h4)h_{5}\notin(h_{1},h_{4}), still h1,h4,h5h_{1},h_{4},h_{5} is not a regular sequence. First we compute the hilbert series of (h1,h4,h5)(h_{1},h_{4},h_{5}) and we find that

HS/(h1,h4,h5)​(t)=1−t−t4+t6+t7−t8(1−t)3.H_{S/(h_{1},h_{4},h_{5})}(t)=\frac{1-t-t^{4}+t^{6}+t^{7}-t^{8}}{(1-t)^{3}}.

If h1,h4,h5h_{1},h_{4},h_{5} were a regular sequence, Hilbert series should have been

HS/(h1,h4,h5)​(t)=(1−t)​(1−t4)​(1−t5)(1−t)3,=1−t−t4+t6+t9−t10(1−t)3,\begin{split}H_{S/(h_{1},h_{4},h_{5})}(t)=&\frac{(1-t)(1-t^{4})(1-t^{5})}{(1-t)^{3}},\\ =&\frac{1-t-t^{4}+t^{6}+t^{9}-t^{10}}{(1-t)^{3}},\end{split}

which is clearly not the case.
